title: Peace in a marriage
hookLine: shalom bayit, lived through daily kindness
tomorrow: the Torah's first 'not good' is being alone. so what about single?

lines: SARAH LAUGHS AT THE TENT DOOR.
cards: Couples argue about the dishwasher, the thermostat, whose turn it is to call the plumber. Now a tent, in the heat of the day. Three visitors tell old Abraham that his wife Sarah will have a son.
Sarah is listening at the tent door, and she laughs to herself. She's worn out, she says, and in the JPS words, "my lord being old also." Then God speaks to Abraham, and repeats what Sarah said.

teach.h: I AM OLD. NOT MY HUSBAND.
teach.b: God asks why Sarah laughed, saying: shall I really bear a child, when I am old? I am old. Not my husband is old.
The line about Abraham is gone.

teach.h: GREAT IS PEACE: EVEN GOD CHANGED A WORD.
teach.b: The Talmud, in Yevamot, notices the change and draws a startling lesson: great is peace, for even the Holy One changed a word for its sake. The tradition's name for it is shalom bayit, peace in the home.

The rabbis take it seriously enough that, in another passage, if a person can afford only one light on a Friday that's also Hanukkah, the Shabbat candle comes first, because it brings peace to the home.
Light to eat by, so no one stumbles or snaps in the dark. Notice what shalom bayit is made of in these stories: small things. One phrase left out.
Not a grand gesture once a year, but quiet edits all day long: the comment you don't pass along, the light left on for someone coming home late, the dish done before anyone asks. And one honest line.
The tradition never asks anyone to buy peace with their own safety. Shalom bayit is peace two people make together, not a silence one of them keeps.

how: Jewish teachers and counselors speak of shalom bayit as a value couples work at together; Shabbat candles lit on Friday evening are linked in the Talmud to peace in the home.

games.q: what does “peace in a marriage” mean?
o: a rule that couples must never argue in public
shalom bayit: the daily work of peace at home
a vow of silence a couple makes at their wedding

games.q: small edits, big peace — tap the pairs.

s: God repeats Sarah's words to Abraham exactly
God leaves out 'my lord being old' and says 'I am old'.
the Talmud puts a Shabbat candle before a Hanukkah candle, for peace at home
shalom bayit means one partner keeps quiet to avoid fights
it's peace two people make; never bought with someone's safety.

games.q: your roommates are fighting about lights left on. one of them says something cutting about the other to you. with Genesis 18 in mind, what do you do?
o: keep the cutting line to yourself; pass on only what helps.
repeat it word for word, so everything is out in the open.
tell both of them it's not your problem and stay out.
games.why: God repeated Sarah's question and left out the hurtful part. Yevamot: great is peace.

practice: Listen to the sounds of the place you live right now: a fridge humming, a door, someone moving in another room, or only your own breath. Let each one be the sound of a shared home.
Then choose one small edit you could make there today: a word left unsaid, a light left on, a kindness done first.

wordCard.voice: Peace in a marriage: shalom bayit, peace at home, made of small edits and small lights.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace of the house, peace at home.

carryVoice: Your line: peace at home, one small edit at a time. Day nine of home and family, kept.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b (great is peace, for even the Holy One changed a word)
Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 23b (the Shabbat lamp before the Hanukkah lamp, because of shalom bayit), with Rashi
